page_contents_html:
Eating disorders in adults

Eating disorders are serious mental illnesses that can cause life-threatening physical complications at any weight. They include anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder (BED), other specified feeding or eating disorder (OSFED) and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID).

Assess and refer early. Do not use BMI, appearance, illness duration or a screening score alone to decide whether someone has an eating disorder, how unwell they are or whether to refer.

Medical or psychiatric emergency

Arrange immediate or same-day emergency assessment if there is a MEED red flag, rapid deterioration, severe dehydration or malnutrition, significant electrolyte disturbance, organ compromise, diabetic ketoacidosis, haematemesis, severe self-harm or high suicide risk. A person may look well and have a normal BMI despite serious instability.

This pathway supports initial assessment and referral. It does not replace the full MEED guidance or local emergency protocols.

accordion_sections.heading: Recognise a possible eating disorder
accordion_sections.html:
Consider an eating disorder in people of any age, sex, gender, ethnicity or body size. Presentations may be indirect and weight may be low, within the expected range or high.

  • Restriction, fasting, avoidance of food groups, ritualised eating, binge eating, self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, insulin restriction, excessive or driven exercise, water loading or use of weight-control medicines.
  • Rapid or unexplained weight change; faltering growth in younger people; marked concern about weight, shape or food; social withdrawal around eating.
  • Dizziness, fainting, weakness, palpitations, cold intolerance, gastrointestinal or menstrual/endocrine symptoms, dental erosion, parotid swelling or unexplained electrolyte disturbance/hypoglycaemia.
  • Depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, self-harm, suicidality, autism or other neurodivergence, substance use, trauma or marked functional decline.
  • Poorly controlled diabetes, recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis or unexplained insulin omission.

SCOFF: a brief screen, not a diagnostic test

Ask the five SCOFF questions where helpful: self-induced Sickness; loss of Control over eating; loss of more than One stone in 3 months; feeling Fat despite others saying the person is too thin; and whether Food dominates life. Two or more “yes” answers raises suspicion, but a lower score does not exclude an eating disorder.

Do not use SCOFF, BMI or laboratory results in isolation. If an eating disorder is suspected after clinical assessment, refer promptly for specialist assessment.

accordion_sections.heading: Immediate risk and same-day action
accordion_sections.html:
Use the MEED traffic-light framework. Risk is multifactorial: one red factor or several amber factors should prompt urgent specialist discussion and a low threshold for acute assessment/admission.

Red flags suggesting impending risk to life

  • Rapid weight loss, including more than 1 kg/week for 2 consecutive weeks; very low weight (BMI below 13 in an adult is one red indicator, not a stand-alone admission rule).
  • Acute food or fluid refusal, intake below about 400 kcal/day, severe dehydration or inability to maintain intake.
  • Waking pulse below 40 beats/min; systolic BP below 90 mmHg with syncope or a significant postural fall; core temperature below 35.5°C.
  • Abnormal ECG, including prolonged QTc or arrhythmia; chest pain, palpitations, collapse or signs of cardiac failure.
  • Unable to sit up from lying or rise from a squat; severe weakness, confusion or seizures.
  • Multiple daily vomiting episodes, severe laxative/diuretic misuse, uncontrolled water loading or more than 2 hours/day of exercise while malnourished.
  • Hypoglycaemia below 3.0 mmol/L; potassium below 2.5 mmol/L; clinically important sodium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate or albumin abnormality; raised urea/creatinine; transaminases more than 3 times normal; or other significant biochemical/haematological abnormality.
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis, haematemesis, gastrointestinal perforation or another life-threatening medical condition.
  • Severe self-harm, high suicide risk, poor insight or fear-driven resistance that prevents life-preserving care.

What to do

  • Immediately life-threatening: call 999 and arrange acute medical care.
  • Medically unstable or uncertain: discuss same day with acute medicine/emergency care and the relevant mental health/eating-disorder clinician. Do not delay because BMI is normal or blood tests were previously normal.
  • Acute suicide or mental health risk without medical instability: use the local Crisis Team/unscheduled-care pathway.
  • If essential treatment is refused and life is at risk, obtain urgent senior psychiatric and medical advice and consider the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003.

accordion_sections.heading: Initial primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
History

  • Onset and course; current and previous weight; amount and rate of weight change; restriction, bingeing, vomiting, laxatives/diuretics, insulin or medication manipulation, fluid intake and exercise.
  • Typical daily intake and duration of little or no intake. Ask about alcohol, substances, caffeine/energy drinks and non-prescribed medicines.
  • Fainting, dizziness, weakness, chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness, cold intolerance, abdominal pain/distension, haematemesis, constipation/diarrhoea, seizures and cognitive change.
  • Depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, self-harm, suicide risk, safeguarding, capacity, social support and effect on daily functioning.
  • Diabetes, pregnancy/postnatal status, coeliac disease, gastrointestinal disease, endocrine disease, renal/cardiac disease, osteoporosis/fracture, neurodivergence and current medicines.
  • Ask the person what would make examination and weighing safer; consider blind weighing and involve family/carers where appropriate and with consent.

Examination

  • Weight, height and BMI, interpreted with weight trajectory and percentage change rather than alone.
  • Pulse, lying and standing blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, hydration, peripheral circulation and oedema.
  • Cardiovascular examination; muscle strength (including ability to sit up/rise from a squat); signs of vomiting, laxative misuse, malnutrition or another physical cause.
  • Record mental state, suicide/self-harm risk and clinical concern even when observations appear reassuring.

accordion_sections.heading: Investigations and medication safety
accordion_sections.html:
Tailor tests to the presentation and urgency. Baseline assessment will commonly include:

  • FBC; urea, creatinine and electrolytes including bicarbonate; calcium, magnesium and phosphate; glucose; LFTs; albumin/total protein.
  • Amylase where recurrent vomiting is suspected; CK where excessive exercise or muscle injury is a concern; TFT and other tests when clinically indicated.
  • 12-lead ECG where there is rapid weight loss, severe purging, bradycardia, hypotension, weakness, electrolyte disturbance, excessive exercise, previous arrhythmia or use of medicines that may affect cardiac function.
  • Pregnancy test, ketones, venous blood gas or diabetes investigations where relevant.

Normal blood tests do not exclude serious risk. Review the whole MEED assessment and repeat investigations according to change in symptoms, intake, purging, observations and the agreed shared-care plan.

Medication review

  • Review medicines that prolong QT, lower blood pressure, disturb electrolytes, suppress appetite or increase sedation/falls risk.
  • Ask specifically about laxatives, diuretics, weight-loss products, stimulants, insulin omission and non-prescribed supplements.
  • Malnutrition and purging can change medicine effectiveness and adverse-effect risk. Seek pharmacy/specialist advice where needed.

accordion_sections.heading: Referral route for adults
accordion_sections.html:
Suspected eating disorder: complete the initial physical and mental health assessment and refer promptly to the relevant adult Community Mental Health Team (CMHT) through SCI Gateway, clearly identifying a possible eating disorder.

  • For a priority referral, telephone the relevant CMHT duty worker first and then submit the electronic referral.
  • CMHT assessment will determine the treatment plan and whether Specialist Eating Disorder Service (SEDS), dietetic, psychology, psychiatric or more intensive input is required.
  • Do not retain a person in primary care solely because BMI is above a threshold, SCOFF is negative, motivation is uncertain or the illness appears “mild”.
  • If risk is rising while awaiting assessment, contact the CMHT duty worker/specialist service and escalate urgency; use acute medical or crisis routes when indicated.

Other routes

  • Under 18: use the local CAMHS pathway. For 16- to 18-year-olds already in care or approaching transition, coordinate directly between services and document who holds responsibility.
  • Pregnancy or postnatal: involve maternity/perinatal mental health services and the eating-disorder pathway.
  • Diabetes: arrange joint working with diabetes and mental health/eating-disorder clinicians; same-day assessment may be required if insulin is omitted, ketones are present or control is deteriorating.

See the DGRefHelp Community Mental Health Teams page for locality contacts, priority discussion and crisis routes.

accordion_sections.heading: What to include in the referral
accordion_sections.html:
• Presenting eating-disorder symptoms and behaviours, onset, duration, weight trajectory and rate of change.
  • Current weight, height and BMI, while making clear that risk is not based on BMI alone.
  • Pulse, lying/standing BP, temperature, hydration, muscle strength and other examination findings.
  • Blood results, ECG report and action already taken; attach or state dates.
  • Current intake and fluid restriction; vomiting, laxative/diuretic use, exercise, water loading, insulin/medicine manipulation.
  • MEED risk factors and the clinician’s overall concern, including any recent deterioration.
  • Mental state, self-harm/suicide risk, capacity, safeguarding, alcohol/substance use and relevant comorbidity.
  • Pregnancy/postnatal status, diabetes, neurodivergence, current medicines and allergies.
  • Family/carer involvement, social support, functional impact, previous treatment and any barriers or reasonable adjustments needed for engagement.

accordion_sections.heading: Monitoring while awaiting assessment or in shared care
accordion_sections.html:
Monitoring frequency must be individualised using MEED risk, current behaviours and the rate of change. Fixed “low/moderate/high” schedules from the former enhanced-service specification should not be used.

  • Agree and document which service holds clinical responsibility, who undertakes physical observations and tests, who reviews results, and how deterioration is escalated.
  • Review sooner after any change in intake, vomiting/purging, exercise, medication, weight trajectory, observations, bloods, ECG, mental state or engagement.
  • Provide clear instructions about whom to contact and when to seek urgent help. Consider proactive contact after missed appointments; non-attendance may increase risk.
  • Primary care should not be left holding sole medical responsibility for a significant or severe eating disorder unless this has been explicitly agreed with specialist clinicians.

For anorexia nervosa in a person not receiving ongoing eating-disorder treatment, offer at least an annual physical and mental health review, while escalating sooner according to clinical need.

accordion_sections.heading: Treatment and support
accordion_sections.html:
Treatment should be person-centred, trauma-informed, multidisciplinary and matched to diagnosis, risk, development, comorbidity and preference.

  • Most people are treated as outpatients, with access to higher-intensity outreach, day or inpatient care when risk or need increases.
  • For adults with anorexia nervosa, evidence-based options include eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED), MANTRA and specialist supportive clinical management (SSCM). Treatment choice is made with the specialist team.
  • Adults with bulimia nervosa are generally offered bulimia-focused guided self-help or CBT-ED; adults with BED are generally offered binge-eating-focused guided self-help or CBT-ED.
  • Dietetic assessment and nutritional rehabilitation should be integrated with psychological and medical care. Medication is not the sole treatment for anorexia nervosa.
  • Uncertainty, ambivalence or fluctuating motivation should prompt skilled engagement and proactive follow-up, not automatic exclusion or discharge.
  • SEDS can provide multidisciplinary assessment, day-programme/meal support, consultation and in-reach according to local criteria and individual need.

Refeeding in a medically compromised person requires an acute/specialist protocol with dietetic and medical oversight. Follow MEED and avoid both refeeding syndrome and harmful underfeeding; do not use the calorie schedules in the former 2008 enhanced-service document.

accordion_sections.heading: Physical health follow-up
accordion_sections.html:
Bone health

  • Weight restoration and treatment of the eating disorder are the main approaches to preventing and treating low bone mineral density.
  • In adults, consider bone-density scanning after 2 years of underweight, or earlier with bone pain or recurrent fractures. Do not arrange routine baseline DEXA solely because BMI is below 17.5.
  • Do not repeat bone-density scanning more often than annually unless bone pain or recurrent fractures develop. Seek osteoporosis/endocrine advice for interpretation or drug treatment.

Purging, dental health and exercise

  • Assess fluid/electrolyte balance with vomiting, laxative/diuretic use or water loading. Explain that laxatives and diuretics do not reduce calorie absorption and support gradual cessation where appropriate.
  • Encourage regular dental review. After vomiting, rinse with water or non-acid mouthwash and avoid brushing teeth immediately.
  • Advise stopping excessive or driven exercise. Activity plans should reflect medical stability and individual risk rather than a BMI-only ladder; avoid high-impact activity where osteoporosis or fracture risk is present.
